Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents:
Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games

Jens Lehmann ††thanks: Work done outside of Amazon. Affiliation: Amazon, TU Dresden
Abstract

Frontier language models have recently been reported to write the weights of neural networks directly, without training: weight-space programming (WSP). If they can do so for tasks they have never seen, a model’s understanding of a task could be compiled into a compact network that runs without the model and might be refined by training. We test this on 20 privately authored, never published game families in the style of ARC-AGI-3. A language model, the writer, receives a game’s simulator source without the held-out levels and must produce one network that plays held-out levels, renderings and start states. When the architecture is fixed (a recurrent convolutional network with 57k parameters), the best writer’s networks solve 56% of episodes on held-out levels with feedback, but the four strongest writers’ Python programs solve 97–100%, and the gap grows with game difficulty. Learning this architecture’s weights from the levels shown to the writers, instead of writing them, transfers far worse (at most 11%), and learned weights fail even on those levels once the rendering changes, which costs written weights at most 8 points. Writers read the source while learners see only those levels, so this compares information access. When writers design their own network in a small tensor language, an exploratory condition, these four writers solve 68–90%. On closer inspection, these networks are programs in network form: 93% of their parameters are exactly zero, 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two, and NumPy programs with the same loop rules and caps solve 91% against the networks’ 79%. In these games, and under a protocol that forbids fitting and search, WSP thus amounts to writing a restricted class of programs, not networks of the kind training produces. Nor does the neural format bring its main hoped-for benefit, training. The best writer’s architectures, trained from standard initialisation within our budget, solve 1%. Written weights in the fixed network are also fragile: weight noise the size of PPO’s first update removes most of their success, as does the update itself. Asked for noise-robust weights, two of three writers tolerate about 10410^{4} times more noise, but PPO’s first update on them is 10–100 times larger and still removes most of their success. With standard PPO on these binary-success games, writing and RL fine-tuning do not combine.

1 Introduction

Frontier language models can solve tasks they have never seen by writing programs, for example programs that play new games. A stranger claim is that they can also write the weights of a neural network directly: construct networks for simple tasks, read what small networks compute, and repair failures by editing parameters (Takehi et al., 2026; Singh, 2026). If such weight-space programming (WSP) works, a model’s reasoning about a task could be compiled into a compact neural agent. Such an agent would run without the model, with small, fixed computation per step instead of a large model’s long and variable reasoning, and, being differentiable, might be refined by reinforcement learning (RL). We find that written networks do not behave like trained ones: they are programs in network form, their architectures fail when trained from scratch within our budget, and written fixed-actor weights do not survive standard PPO fine-tuning.

We are interested in three research questions about WSP. Do written networks generalise to instances their writer never saw? Do they add anything over an ordinary program written by the same model, for example because they can be trained further or run more cheaply? Do they add anything over learning the same network from the instances the writer was shown? Existing demonstrations use public tasks (Breakout, Go, arithmetic), where recall of familiar strategies cannot be excluded, and rarely compare against programs or against learning in the same architecture.

We study these questions on 20 privately authored game families in the style of ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026). Games are a demanding test: a player must read the frame, remember what it has done and act over many steps, and new levels show whether it generalises. We report the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games as a separate, possibly familiar tier. In our setup, a language model, the writer, receives a game’s simulator source with solvers and held-out levels removed. The remaining support levels are the ones it can study and get feedback on. It must produce one actor that plays held-out levels, renderings and start states. Nine writer models from OpenAI and Anthropic either set the weights of a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent convolutional actor, design and set a network of their own in a small tensor language (free architecture, FreeArch), or write a Python player, each one-shot or with feedback. We compare against learned weights in the same actor and against simple replay and fixed-action baselines.

Findings.

  1. 1.

    In the fixed actor, written weights generalise, but programs are far better. Main writers’ actors solve 33–56% of held-out-level episodes with feedback, far above the baselines (≤4%{\leq}4\%), while their Python players solve 97–100%, and the gap grows with difficulty. Where a program can solve the task, as here, writing it is the better approach. Tasks without a compact program may differ.

  2. 2.

    Learned weights in the fixed actor transfer poorly, and written weights are appearance-invariant. Learning the actor’s weights from the support levels, instead of writing them, transfers at most 11%, although the actor can fit held-out episodes when trained on them. The learned actors fail even on the levels they were trained on once the rendering changes: a held-out renderer template alone costs them 34–79 points and written weights 1–8. Writers read the source and learners see 15–30 level starts per family, so this compares information access more than learning.

  3. 3.

    With a free architecture, writers write programs in network form. In networks of their own design, an exploratory condition, main writers solve 68–90%, mostly owing to the free topology. The networks are bounded, branch-free tensor programs, and NumPy programs with the same loop rules and caps do better (91% against 79%). Writers had to construct weights by design, without fitting or search, which favours such networks. The ability is concentrated in the strongest models: the other current and the previous-generation writers reach only 14–48%.

  4. 4.

    The ordering holds on the public games. On the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, which are harder and possibly familiar, programs (43–75%) beat free architectures (13–42%), which beat fixed-actor weights (≤8%{\leq}8\%).

  5. 5.

    Written weights and standard PPO do not combine. In the fixed actor, written weights do not survive PPO fine-tuning: weight noise the size of PPO’s first update removes most of their success, and PPO removes it, as does a random update of the same size. The writers’ architectures also fail when trained from scratch within our budget (1% for the best writer). So the main hoped-for benefit of the neural format is not realised here, and written networks are also slower per step than Python players.

Contributions.

The findings above are our main contribution. They rest on (i) a controlled protocol for weight-space programming on unseen interactive tasks: audited mechanics-only sources, held-out final levels, certified perturbed starts, closed-loop controls and complete request accounting for the main study; (ii) a multi-writer comparison of written weights, in a fixed actor and in free architectures, with programs by the same models, learned weights in the same actor, and controls that separate the language, the topology and the operators; and (iii) tests of training from scratch, refinement by RL and cost, with weight-perturbation controls.

2 Related work

Weight-space programming.

Takehi et al. (2026) report that a frontier model can tell from raw weights what a small network was trained to do, write MinAtar and 9×99\times 9 Go policy networks from the rules, and repair networks by direct edits. Their games are public. Singh (2026) had a coding agent set every weight of small transformers for ten algorithmic tasks, and document evaluation leakage, forbidden fitting and lookup-table solutions, which motivate our sandbox and held-out design. A later version also writes language classifiers and brain encoding models (Singh et al., 2026). Follow-up work edits small language models for reasoning benchmarks (Hu et al., 2026) and audits small clinical networks (Nusrat and Nusrat, 2026). On the reading side, Ahmed (2026) find that zero-shot weight reading relies on local arithmetic and dataset priors more than on tracing computation. We differ from this work in four ways. Our games are private, so writers cannot recall solutions, and every network is scored on held-out levels, renderings and start states. Each written network is compared with programs by the same model and with weights learned in the same architecture. We test whether written networks can be trained further, with RL and perturbation controls. And we cover nine writers across two model generations, in a fixed architecture and in architectures the writers design.

Rules and programs compiled into networks.

KBANN maps a propositional domain theory to the topology and initial weights of a network (Towell and Shavlik, 1994), finite-state automata can be programmed stably into recurrent networks (Omlin and Giles, 1996), and neural-symbolic work generalises such translations (d’Avila Garcez et al., 2002; Besold et al., 2017). A minimal convolutional network can run the Game of Life exactly, yet networks of that size rarely learn it (Springer and Kenyon, 2021), and gradient descent in differentiable interpreters rarely finds the programs that discrete search finds (Gaunt et al., 2016). RASP and Tracr compile programs into transformer weights (Weiss et al., 2021; Lindner et al., 2023), with extensions to learnable (Friedman et al., 2023), looped (Shaw et al., 2025; Giannou et al., 2023) and embedded (Weng et al., 2024) programs. There, a person or an exact compiler translates a formal rule language. Our writers start from simulator source, must also invent the policy, and give no correctness guarantee: we measure correctness on held-out instances.

Generating weights.

HyperNetworks (Ha et al., 2017), G.pt (Peebles et al., 2022), p-diff (Wang et al., 2024b), neural functionals (Navon et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023) and Text-to-LoRA (Charakorn et al., 2025) learn a mapping into weight space by gradient descent, mostly from collections of trained networks (Wang et al., 2026, see also). Our writers receive no trained networks or gradients, only the task’s source and feedback.

Algorithmic reasoning in networks.

CLRS (Veličković et al., 2022; Veličković and Blundell, 2021), value iteration networks (Tamar et al., 2016) and weight-tied recurrent networks that extrapolate by iterating longer (Schwarzschild et al., 2021; Bansal et al., 2022) ask whether gradient descent finds algorithmic solutions. We ask whether a writer can set them directly. Our fixed actor contains such a weight-tied recurrent block, iterated 128 times per step, so a writer can use it to run an iterative algorithm, for example to spread information across the grid.

Language models writing code that acts.

Language models write robot policies (Liang et al., 2023), skill libraries (Wang et al., 2024a), reward functions (Ma et al., 2024), world models (Tang et al., 2024; Dainese et al., 2024), evolved programs (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), programmatic policies (Liu et al., 2025) and game-playing algorithms (Li et al., 2026). On ARC (Chollet, 2019; Chollet et al., 2025), sampled and verified programs are among the strongest approaches (Wang et al., 2024c; Li et al., 2025; Chollet et al., 2024). ARC-AGI-3 turns such tasks into games that require exploration and rule discovery (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026), where coding agents build programmatic world models from interaction (Lehmann et al., 2026) and training-free graph exploration is a strong baseline (Rudakov et al., 2025). Our writers instead read the game’s source, so we measure how well they compile known rules. The weights conditions ask for the program as the parameters of a network, so that no language-model call, planner or search remains at run time.

RL fine-tuning and distillation.

Fine-tuning can forget capabilities on states that are not visited early (Wołczyk et al., 2024), which JSRL (Uchendu et al., 2023) and residual policy learning (Silver et al., 2018; Johannink et al., 2019) avoid by keeping the prior policy fixed. Our distillation baseline builds on policy distillation (Rusu et al., 2015; Czarnecki et al., 2019; Hinton et al., 2015) and DAgger (Ross et al., 2011).

3 Experimental setup

3.1 Games and held-out scope

We study generalisation within a game: given a game’s rules, the writer must produce one actor that plays new levels, layouts, renderings and states of that game. Games the writer was never told about are left for future work. “Unseen” refers to the writer: the private games were never published, although familiar ideas such as path finding, parity and matching are known to the models.

Private tier (primary).

20 ARC-AGI-3-style game families (Table 7, Appendix A.7). An observation is a 64×6464\times 64 grid of 16 colour ids. The actions are RESET, ACTION1–5, ACTION6 (a click at a cell) and ACTION7. Before any result, the game author assigned each family to a difficulty stratum: 3 easy, 11 medium, 5 hard and 1 very hard. Core computations include object comparison, colour matching under a budget, maze planning with global phase changes, click localisation with cascades, constraint covering, timing and hidden state. Each family has 6–12 fixed levels and ten renderer templates that keep the mechanics but vary geometry, object and HUD grammar, and palette. A held-out template is not an interpolation of the shown ones, and the colour ids that carry a role change across templates and palettes, so a detector keyed to fixed colour ids cannot work (Figure 1 shows an example, Appendix A.7). Every family comes with an exact planner that we wrote, a solver that returns a shortest action sequence completing a level from a given state. It certifies evaluation instances and supervises or shapes learned baselines, but is never used in the writer or actor. Three of the 20 families (ztl, lys, esm) were used in a preliminary study that informed the protocol and prompts (Appendix A.4).

Public tier (secondary).

The 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games are widely discussed, so writers may know them, and we report them separately. They have no renderer templates, so each game has a single rendering.

Splits and evaluation sets.

For a game with nn levels we hold out levels n,n−2,…n,n-2,\dots down to level 2: about half the levels, always including the final one. Templates 0–4 are shown and 5–9 held out. The primary set, Q-lvl, contains every held-out level under all ten templates, each from the level’s start and from up to five certified perturbed starts. A perturbed start is reached by 1–6 random actions that change the observation. It is kept only if the planner’s direct plan from it replays to completion. We report held-out levels between shown ones (Q-lvl-mid) and the final level (Q-lvl-final) separately. Q-tpl renders support levels with held-out templates, and S-start holds the support level starts used for feedback. On the public tier, each held-out level has its start and up to 20 perturbed starts. An episode ends on level completion (success), on GAME_OVER or after 3×3\times(certified plan length)+10+10 actions; RESET restarts the level and counts as an action. All sets are built mechanically before the main study’s first writer call (Appendix A.7).

Mechanics-only source.

The writer receives the game’s source code, the simulator that applies actions and renders frames, without held-out level data and template parameters (replaced by WITHHELD placeholders), without any solver, planner or oracle routine or value derived from one, such as optimal move counts, and without comments that discuss levels or strategy. The redacted simulator reproduces the original frame for frame on every support level and template (525k steps), and raises an error when asked to build a held-out level or template, whose data it no longer contains (Appendix A.8). Ablation M+S keeps the solver.

3.2 The fixed actor

All fixed-architecture neural conditions produce the weights of one recurrent convolutional actor with 57,289 float32 parameters (Appendix A.1). We designed it before the study to express the computations grid games need, with operators simple enough to set by hand, not for particular games:

  • •

    one-hot colour planes and coordinate channels, for colours and positions;

  • •

    a 5×55\times 5 and a 3×33\times 3 convolution, for local patterns and objects;

  • •

    row- and column-wise max broadcasts, for same-row and same-column relations;

  • •

    a weight-tied 3×33\times 3 block iterated 128 times, for flood fills and distance fields (Schwarzschild et al., 2021; Bansal et al., 2022; Tamar et al., 2016);

  • •

    spatial pooling, an MLP with a 64-dimensional episodic memory, an action head and a click map, for decisions that depend on earlier steps.

Decoding is deterministic argmax over available actions. The actor runs alone, without search, planner or external calls, at 1.32 GMAC per step. Final actor evaluations use exact FP32; the training-time curves in Figure 4 use TF32 checkpoints. Written networks are numerically brittle: TF32 convolutions change the decisions of 11 of 60 tested written actors (Appendix A.9).

3.3 Free architecture

In the free-architecture condition (FreeArch), the writer designs its own network in a small static tensor language and supplies all of its weights. We specified the language after the fixed-actor results were known, so the FreeArch analyses are exploratory. The language offers convolutions, elementwise arithmetic including multiplication and min/max, row, column and global pooling, dense layers, weight-tied loops of fixed length and an episodic memory, but no data-dependent control flow. Inputs are the fixed actor’s plus the available-action mask. Caps on graph size, loop length, arithmetic (1.5 GMAC per step, close to the fixed actor’s 1.33) and parameters (150k, 2.6×\times the fixed actor’s) match the two settings roughly on arithmetic, not on parameters or wall-clock cost (Appendix A.1). The prompt shows the fixed actor in the language as an example.

Two controls separate what FreeArch changes, with the same writers, families, runs and feedback. In control A, the graph must be the fixed actor’s own graph written in the language, so only the weights are free. In control B, any graph is allowed, but only with the fixed actor’s operations. The bounded program player writes NumPy code under FreeArch’s loop rules and caps, with more operations (division, comparisons, np.where and others) and without node or channel limits (Appendix A.1). It shows what the weight format costs against a program with the same limits.

3.4 Writers and conditions

Writers.

The four main writers are GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Opus 5.5. The five weaker writers are GPT-6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5 and the previous-generation GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5. All run at reasoning effort high, without tools, with the same prompt: the mechanics-only source and the engine base class, the support start observations, the episode rules and, for the weights conditions, the actor’s exact NumPy reference (Appendices A.3 and A.4).

Conditions

(Figure 1).

  • •

    Written weights, one-shot (W1) or with feedback (W2): the writer returns build(), which constructs all tensors of the fixed actor. A sandbox prohibits training, fitting, searching over weights and simulating the game (Appendix A.5). Feedback allows up to three resubmissions, each after an outcome table on the support starts and up to three failure reports (frames, action traces and, for networks, logits and channel maxima).

  • •

    FreeArch W1 and FreeArch W2: the same in the free architecture.

  • •

    Python players, one-shot (P1) or with feedback (P2): act(obs, available, memory). They control for game understanding.

  • •

    P-react: a one-shot Python player that may not simulate the game or search, with fixed computation per frame and 50 ms per step. It is a program control closer to what a network computes. The restrictions are prompted and audited, not enforced (Appendix A.5).

W1, W2, P1 and both FreeArch arms run for all nine writers and the other arms for the main writers, with three runs per family (Table 9). P-react and the public-tier one-shot arms run for the seven current writers. Ablations on six families, with one run each, add solver code, remove the actor’s axial broadcasts, cut its tied iterations to 8, or lower the reasoning effort.

Hypotheses.

Four hypotheses about the fixed actor on the private tier, and the fixed-actor analyses, were written down in a protocol before data collection (excerpt and dated amendments in the supplement):

  • •

    H1: the main writers’ written weights solve held-out instances well above the replay and open-loop floors (Section 3.6).

  • •

    H2: written weights generalise better than weights learned in the same actor from the same support data, with augmentations that the source shows to preserve the game’s rules.

  • •

    H3: weight writing degrades with game difficulty faster than program writing.

  • •

    H4: written actors are closed-loop and do not replay support sequences.

3.5 Learned baselines

All fixed-architecture learned baselines train the identical 57k actor from the same initialisation, on support levels and templates unless noted (Appendix A.6). BC-support is DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) with the planner as teacher. BC-aug adds augmentations that the source shows to preserve the game’s rules: colour permutations, and board symmetries where the game’s own templates use them (a symmetry-only variant runs on 13 families). BC-oracle also trains on states of the held-out levels and is a capacity check, not a generalisation result. Distill and distill-aug use a writer’s final P2 player as teacher, without and with augmentation. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) uses a sparse completion reward (2×1062\times 10^{6} steps), and the privileged PPO-shaped adds potential-based shaping (Ng et al., 1999) from the planner’s distance to go. Learned FreeArch networks are Astra’s FreeArch graphs with re-initialised weights, trained by BC-support and by distillation for at most 6 h per run.

3.6 Evaluation and statistics

Floors and closed-loop controls.

Two floors measure how much of a game can be solved without reading the frame. The replay floor replays, on every held-out start, the planner’s plan for the support start whose first frame differs from it in the fewest cells. The open-loop floor is the best fixed schedule: one action, or two alternating ones, repeated until the episode ends. We would have excluded as blind-solvable any family on which a floor reaches 0.5. None does, and no public game scores above 0. For every written actor we measure success with a constant observation (zero frame) or one frozen at the episode’s first frame (first frame), success on perturbed starts with RESET disabled, and how often the action changes on counterfactual frames.

Scoring and statistics.

Refusals, truncated replies, invalid artifacts and undelivered sessions score 0; Table 18 reports delivery, scores without undelivered sessions and other protocol-specified analyses. The unit of analysis is the family: runs are averaged within a family, then families are weighted equally (family macro). Q-lvl success is level-balanced (the mean of per-level success; within 0.02 of the raw episode rate at the reported family-macro cell level). Confidence intervals come from a hierarchical bootstrap over families, held-out levels and runs; paired differences are bootstrapped over families. Appendix A.9 covers numerics and integrity.

4 Results

4.1 Written weights generalise (H1)

Table 1 gives held-out-level success (Q-lvl) for every writer and condition on the 20 private families. GPT-6 Astra’s written actors solve 40% of held-out-level episodes one-shot (W1) and 56% with feedback (W2). With feedback, GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 43%, Claude Opus 5.5 36% and GPT-6.1 Terra 33%. The other current models solve at most 6% one-shot, and previous-generation models at most 12%. Replaying the plan of the nearest support start solves 2.5%, and the best repeating action schedule 3.9%. No family exceeds 0.26 under the first floor or 0.46 under the second. H1 holds in every difficulty stratum except the very hard family (Table 19). Without the preliminary-study families, W2 is 0.27–0.50 and P2 0.96–1.00 (Table 20).

Every main writer improves with feedback, by 11–21 points and in 15–17 of 20 families. Runs vary widely: 31 of Astra’s 60 feedback runs reach 50% on held-out levels, and 25 of Sol’s. Selection matches part of the feedback gain: the best of three one-shot runs, chosen by support-start success at a similar request count, recovers 45–70% of it (Appendix B).

A new appearance costs almost nothing, a new level costs a lot.

A template keeps a level’s mechanics but can rotate or mirror the board, draw objects and the HUD in another style and give roles other colours. Re-rendering one state under another template changes up to 99% of its cells (median over families of the largest change). Every episode carries its renderer template, so success splits by appearance novelty and level novelty at once (Table 10). Holding the levels and the start type fixed, a held-out template costs written weights 1 point for Astra (−0.01-0.01 [−0.03-0.03, +0.01+0.01], paired over families), 2 for Sol, 4 for Terra and 8 for Opus 5.5, and at most 5 in networks of the writers’ own design. A permuted palette, which changes the colour ids of every role, costs no more. The written actors therefore locate objects from the frame rather than from fixed colours or positions, which they could not read off the source (Section 3.1). Their first layers show how: 73% of the channels that read colour apply one kernel to eight or more colours or repeat one detector for each of four or more colours, whereas every channel of a learned first layer reads all 16 colours with distinct kernels. New levels are the difficulty: on the same held-out templates, success falls from 78% on support levels to 56% on held-out ones for Astra, and held-out levels between shown ones are solved more often than the final level (Astra W2 61% against 40%, Sol 47% against 31%).

Ablations.

On six families with one run each (Table 21, Appendix B), solver code in the source does not clearly help written weights, removing the actor’s axial broadcasts changes little, and cutting its tied iterations from 128 to 8 hurts most.

4.2 Weights versus programs (H3)

Every writer’s Python players beat its written weights: by 39–75 points one-shot, by 44–65 points with feedback for the main writers, and in 76 of the 80 main writer–family pairs with feedback (3 pairs tie and 1 is reversed). H3 was specified as a difficulty-by-format interaction without a fixed test statistic, so we assess it descriptively per stratum (Figure 2; Table 19, with CIs over families). The main writers’ written actors (W2) solve 89% [79, 99] on easy families, 40% [27, 55] on medium, 27% [8, 48] on hard and 0% on the very hard stratum, which is a single family. Python players stay at 96–99% in every stratum, so with P2 near ceiling the growing gap mainly reflects the decline of W2. An exploratory trend test with the family as unit agrees: the per-family P2−-W2 gap rises with stratum rank (Spearman ρ=0.67\rho=0.67, one-sided permutation p<0.001p<0.001, 20 families; without the preliminary-study families ρ=0.59\rho=0.59, p=0.007p=0.007). One-shot, where P1 is below ceiling (Table 19), it gives ρ=0.52\rho=0.52 (p=0.009p=0.009). H3 is supported descriptively.

P-react, the one-shot program control without simulation or search, solves 40% pooled over the main writers: close to written weights with feedback (42%) and far below unrestricted programs (99%). It is not matched to the actor’s computation (Appendix B).

What do these results say about writing weights? Across the nine writers and 20 families, a one-shot network solves at least half of the held-out-level episodes only where the same writer’s one-shot Python player does too (19 of 19 such writer–family pairs in the fixed actor, 51 of 51 with a free architecture, Section 4.3). Where the program fails (34 pairs), the networks solve 2% and 6%. Understanding a game well enough to program it thus appears necessary for writing its weights, and expressing that understanding in a fixed network is the hard part. This does not show that writers derive their weights from a program, since any harder output format could give the same pattern. Programs also handle new templates because the source contains the code of the five support templates and the prompt says that evaluation uses unseen visual variants. Their players parse frames invariantly, for example by taking the most frequent colour as background and matching objects by shape rather than by colour id.

4.3 A free architecture closes most of the gap (FreeArch, exploratory)

Table 2 pairs each writer’s FreeArch networks with its fixed-actor weights, and Figure 2 shows both by difficulty. Every main writer gains 33–41 points with feedback, all confidence intervals above zero, and FreeArch is better in 17–19 of the 20 families. One-shot, FreeArch reaches 40–74%. The collapse with difficulty largely disappears: pooled over the main writers, FreeArch actors solve 95% on easy, 78% on medium, 76% on hard and 64% on the very hard stratum, where the fixed actor reached 0%. Without the preliminary-study families, FreeArch W2 is 65–89% and the gain 37–47 points, every interval above zero (Table 20). As in the fixed actor, the final level is harder (Astra: 81% against 93%).

Gap to programs.

Astra’s FreeArch actors come within 10 points of its Python players, and within 5 points on 12 of the 20 families. Sol 6.1 comes within 16 points, and Terra and Opus 5.5 within 24–28. Neither program control is matched to FreeArch: P2 may simulate and search without bound, P-react may do neither, and FreeArch networks run bounded loops of up to 256 iterations. With FreeArch’s loop rules and caps, the bounded program players solve 91%, against 79% for FreeArch W2 (+0.11+0.11 [+0.06+0.06, +0.17+0.17]; Table 15), with positive point estimates for every writer, although Sol 6.1’s interval includes zero; unrestricted players stay 8 points ahead [4, 12]. The +0.11+0.11 estimates the cost of the weight format, with confounds in both directions (Appendix A.1).

Where the gain comes from

(Table 16, Appendix B).

  • •

    Not the prompt or the language. Control A matches the fixed actor (+0.01+0.01 [−0.02-0.02, +0.04+0.04], pooled over writers); all 240 delivered A graphs equal the fixed actor’s graph.

  • •

    Mostly the topology. Control B gains 29 points over A [21, 37], with every writer’s interval above zero. B is better in all 20 families pooled, and in 16, 19, 17 and 20 families for Astra, Sol 6.1, Opus 5.5 and Terra. 11 of 608 B candidates used other operations and were rejected as invalid.

  • •

    The added operators contribute the rest (+0.06+0.06 [+0.02+0.02, +0.10+0.10]), most clearly for Opus 5.5 (+0.12+0.12).

  • •

    Not the parameter cap. 152 of the 239 delivered FreeArch networks and 108 of the 240 B networks stay within the fixed actor’s 57k parameters and its MACs. These alone solve 80% and 68% of held-out-level episodes, against 42% for the fixed actor on the same families. This comparison selects artifacts after the fact and is descriptive.

The controls do not separate the architecture from the weights written into it.

Weaker writers gain far less.

With feedback, the weaker writers’ FreeArch networks solve 14–48%, against 68–90% for the main writers (Table 2, lower block). FreeArch helps four of the five, by 7–23 points with confidence intervals above zero, but not GPT-6 Luna (+0.04+0.04 [−0.01-0.01, +0.09+0.09]). The weaker writers can still write programs: one-shot, their Python players solve 45–86%, against 6–25% for their FreeArch networks. Writing a working network from the rules is thus concentrated in the strongest models.

What writers build.

The main writers’ 451 delivered private-tier FreeArch networks (one-shot and with feedback) have a median of 30k parameters (interquartile range 11k–64k) and 0.33 GMAC per step (0.07–0.80), less than the fixed actor. They rely heavily on multiplicative gating, which the fixed actor lacks. 320 of them use tied loops of 2–256 iterations (median 48), and 154 read the available-action mask. Their weights are hand-set constants: 93% of all parameters are exactly 0, and 90% of the nonzero ones are ±1\pm 1, another small integer or a power of two (97% and 86% for written fixed-actor weights, W2). They encode Boolean logic, for example NOT as 1−min⁡(relu⁡(x),1)1-\min(\mathrm{relu}(x),1) and AND as a product. They are closed-loop: fed a constant frame instead of the observation, they solve at most 4% of held-out-level episodes. FreeArch networks are thus bounded, branch-free tensor programs in network form, with fixed iteration counts. This is close to compiling programs into networks (Weiss et al., 2021; Lindner et al., 2023), except that the writer, not a compiler, derives the computation from informal rules and source. Nor are they cheaper to run than programs: a FreeArch network takes a median of 5–24 ms per step on a GPU and 36 ms on one CPU thread, against 0.8 ms for a sandboxed Python player (Table 25, Appendix B).

4.4 Written versus learned weights (H2)

Table 3 compares written weights with learned weights in the identical actor. BC-support fits the support starts (95%) but transfers poorly to held-out levels (11%). Distilling the writers’ own Python players fits the teacher on the support levels (92% of support starts), yet solves only 10% of held-out-level episodes, where the teachers solve over 99% (Figure 3, Appendix B). PPO with sparse reward reaches 8%. The privileged PPO-shaped baseline fits the support set only partly and transfers no better (5%). With source-licensed augmentation, the learners fail to fit the support set within our training budget: they solve only 17–20% of support starts (BC-aug, distill-aug; 56% with dihedral transformations alone) and 7–10% of held-out-level episodes. Per family, Astra’s written actors beat the best non-privileged learned baseline by 41 points [29, 54], and in 18 of the 20 families (both are near zero in the other two). H2 is supported, as a comparison of information access: writers read the source, while learners see only the support levels (15–30 starts per family and their perturbations). The learners with augmentation, which H2 names, did not fit their training levels, which weakens the comparison. The result shows that support-level data do not convey what the source does; it is not a test of learning as such.

The learned actors also fail without any new level. On the support levels, where BC-support solves 92% under the templates it trained on, a held-out template alone drops it to 13% (−0.79-0.79 [−0.86-0.86, −0.72-0.72]; distillation −0.74-0.74, PPO −0.34-0.34; Table 10), against −0.01-0.01 for Astra’s written weights. The one learner that is appearance-robust, BC-aug, buys it from palette and dihedral augmentation licensed by the source, and fits the support set so poorly (20%) that it gains nothing overall.

The actor can fit these episodes when trained on them. Trained with the planner teacher on states from all levels, including the held-out levels’ own start states (BC-oracle), it solves 90% of held-out-level episodes. This is an in-distribution capacity check, not generalisation, and it isolates the appearance effect: BC-oracle trains on all ten templates and is robust to them (+0.02+0.02), yet a permuted palette, which it never sees, drops it from 90% to 26%, where written weights lose nothing (+0.01+0.01 for Astra, paired over families). A learned actor of this architecture can therefore reach the written actors’ accuracy and still not survive a change of appearance.

Learned FreeArch networks.

A writer’s own graphs learn almost nothing when trained from standard initialisation. With re-initialised weights, Astra’s FreeArch graphs solve 1% of held-out-level episodes under BC-support or distillation, against 89% with Astra’s written weights (+0.89+0.89 [+0.77+0.77, +0.98+0.98]; Table 17, Appendix B), although the same learners fit the support set in the fixed actor. These graphs are hard-gated circuits built for hand-set constants: many have no gradient at initialisation and others diverge. They are thus not trainable from standard initialisation within our budget, which does not show that no learner could fit them.

4.5 Closed-loop behaviour and mechanism (H4)

The main writers’ W2 actors read the screen and act closed-loop (Table 22, Appendix B). With a constant frame they solve at most 2% of held-out episodes, and frozen at the first frame 5–7%. On perturbed starts without RESET they solve 41–65%, and their action changes on 71–76% of counterfactual frames. H4 holds.

Mechanism.

In five strong written actors, we ablated the components the writers name, after writing down the predicted effect. 14 of 17 predictions were confirmed: for example, zeroing the tied-block channels a writer calls a flood fill drops held-out success from 0.97 to 0 (Appendix B).

4.6 Public games

On the 25 public games, which are harder and possibly familiar (Tables 23 and 24, Appendix B), fixed-actor written weights fail: at most 8% on held-out levels for every writer and condition. Free architectures help (13–42% with feedback, gains of 7–34 points), but they stay about 30 points below the same writers’ Python players (43–75%). Possible familiarity does not rescue weight writing, and the larger residual gap suggests that richer mechanics are harder to compile.

4.7 Weight writing and standard PPO: no benefit in either direction

From written weights to RL.

We fine-tuned the W2 actors of Astra, Sol 6.1 and Terra on the six ablation families with PPO (3 seeds, 300k steps, sparse and planner-shaped reward; Figure 4, Appendix B). Final actors are evaluated in exact FP32, and diverged runs score 0. Written actors work on ztl, lys and esm (Astra’s also on ruz) and start near 0 on crg and mds, so the result rests mainly on three to four families, three of them from the preliminary study. Standard PPO drives held-out success from 0.50 at initialisation to 0.01. Structure-preserving PPO (Appendix A.6) ends at 0.08–0.10, and small-step SGD at 0.22–0.25: success improves as the step size shrinks. RL from the learned baselines’ initialisation θ0\theta_{0} and from matched-random initialisations stays at 0.02 or below. Under the decision rule specified before data collection, no family, writer, variant and reward combination beats both the written initialisation and RL(θ0\theta_{0}) (0 of 132). Standard PPO collapses by its first checkpoint (16k steps), also in exact FP32 and on support starts, and rescaling the output head does not help (Appendix A.6). The main cause is fragility (Table 4): random noise of 10−710^{-7} of each tensor’s RMS already removes much of the success, at this size mostly through the exact zeros, although decisions are not near ties. PPO’s first checkpoint moves the weights by 10−410^{-4} overall, and a random update of the same size and support is as destructive.

Robust written weights.

Asked for weights robust to noise of 10−310^{-3} of each tensor’s RMS, Astra and Sol 6.1 lose 3 and 8 points but keep most of their success up to that noise, about 10410^{4} times what halves standard weights (Table 13; Opus 5.5 does not become robust). PPO still removes their success (Table 14): its first update on them is 10–100 times larger, about as destructive as a random update of that size.

From RL to written weights.

Asked to repair RL-trained actors by editing weights, Astra and Sol 6.1 rebuild them to the level of their fresh W2 actors, while continued PPO stays at 0.00–0.01 (Appendix B).

5 Conclusions

Given the mechanics of an unpublished game, the strongest current language models can write the weights of a network that plays new levels, renderings and start states of that game, closed-loop and far above replaying plans or repeating actions. Written weights also generalise better than weights learned in the same network from the levels the writers saw, because the source tells the writer what the support levels do not.

What the writers produce, however, are programs in network form. With a free architecture, the main writers write bounded, branch-free tensor programs that come close to their own Python programs but not beyond them. In the fixed architecture they fall far short: 145 of 240 main-writer feedback runs stay below 50% on held-out levels, although the same actor fits these episodes when trained on them. Nor do written networks combine with training here: the architectures fail when trained from scratch, and a single standard PPO update removes most of the fixed actor’s success, even with noise-robust weights. Where a task can be solved by a program, as here, writing the program remains the better choice.

These results suggest a hypothesis about how weight-space programming works: the writer first derives a symbolic solution and then expresses it in weights, so that what it writes is a program even when the output is a network. Earlier demonstrations fit this reading. Takehi et al. (2026) describe their writer as converting “desired programs” into neural form for public games with known rules, and where no algorithm is known, written models are built from hand-designed interpretable features (Singh et al., 2026). Their written transformers for language tasks have the same signature as our networks: rebuilding 21 of their 24 released language-task models from their code, we find 99% of the parameters exactly zero and 95% of the rest small integers or powers of two (Appendix B). Our evidence comes from games whose perception, although it must be computed at run time, can be specified exactly from the rendering code, and whose policies admit a compact program. Tasks whose perception is statistical rather than exact, such as natural images, would test the hypothesis, and tasks with dense rewards, where RL fine-tuning works well, would test whether writing and training can combine.

Limitations.

  • •

    Scope. We test generalisation within a game family, with the mechanics given as source code, not the discovery of unknown rules or transfer to new games. Our games have binary success per level, which makes them a poor testbed for combining writing with RL. The RL result covers standard PPO on the fixed actor with from-scratch settings, with structure-preserving PPO and small-step SGD controls but without supervised fine-tuning, and rests on three to four families (Section 4.7).

  • •

    Estimation. Per-family estimates rest on 3–6 held-out levels, and the ablations use one run each. Learning budgets were bounded (2M PPO steps, 6 DAgger iterations, 6 h per learned FreeArch network), so stronger learners might narrow the gap to written weights.

  • •

    Independence and elicitation. The games were authored with language-model assistance and never published. Prompts were piloted with evaluated writers, only the Claude writers get a task-budget hint, and refused Opus 5.5 sessions score 0. An evaluated writer (Claude Opus 5.5) designed the harness and analysis. Writers had no tools and had to construct weights by design, which favours program-like networks.
