  • Zhou et al. (2023) Allan Zhou, Kaien Yang, Kaylee Burns, Adriano Cardace, Yiding Jiang, Samuel Sokota, J. Zico Kolter, and Chelsea Finn. Permutation equivariant neural functionals. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2023.

Appendix A Reproducibility details

This appendix specifies the actor, episodes, prompts, writer settings, sandbox, learned baselines, evaluation sets and redaction procedure, and summarises evaluation numerics and integrity. All evaluation sets and redacted game sections were fixed before the main study’s first writer call, and each condition’s prompts before its first call.

Release.

Code and compact result data are available in the project repository (commit 20eee09). The release contains the evaluation and writer harness, the code that builds every prompt, the free-architecture language with its validator and executors, the public-tier query manifests, and per-session results and request accounting for the main-study conditions, with a script that recomputes the headline numbers. The robustness follow-up has aggregate noise curves, per-run PPO results and matched-random-update evaluations. The sources and level data of the 20 private families are withheld so that they stay unseen. On request, we evaluate submitted actors and players on them.

A.1 Actor specification

Table 5 lists every tensor of the fixed actor. One step computes, with ⋆\star a convolution, 1×11\times 1 maps written as matrix products over channels, and T=128T=128:

F1\displaystyle F_{1} =ReLU⁡(W1⋆x0+b1),F2=ReLU⁡(W2⋆F1+b2),\displaystyle=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{1}\star x_{0}+b_{1}),\qquad F_{2}=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{2}\star F_{1}+b_{2}),
F3\displaystyle F_{3} =ReLU⁡(W3​[F2;rowmax⁡(F2);colmax⁡(F2)]+b3),\displaystyle=\mathrm{ReLU}\big(W_{3}\,[F_{2};\,\mathrm{rowmax}(F_{2});\,\mathrm{colmax}(F_{2})]+b_{3}\big),
H(0)\displaystyle H^{(0)} =0,H(t)=ReLU(Wh⋆H(t−1)+UhF3+bh),t=1,…,T,H=H(T),\displaystyle=0,\qquad H^{(t)}=\mathrm{ReLU}\big(W_{h}\star H^{(t-1)}+U_{h}F_{3}+b_{h}\big),\quad t=1,\dots,T,\qquad H=H^{(T)},
g\displaystyle g =[max⁡H;mean​H;max⁡F3;mean​F3]∈ℝ96,z=ReLU⁡(Wz​g+bz),\displaystyle=[\max H;\ \mathrm{mean}\,H;\ \max F_{3};\ \mathrm{mean}\,F_{3}]\in\mathbb{R}^{96},\qquad z=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{z}g+b_{z}),
m′\displaystyle m^{\prime} =tanh⁡(Wm​m+Wm​z​z+Wm​a​a−+bm),ℓ=Wo​[z;m′]+bo,κ=Wc​[F3;H]+bc.\displaystyle=\tanh(W_{m}m+W_{mz}z+W_{ma}a^{-}+b_{m}),\qquad\ell=W_{o}[z;m^{\prime}]+b_{o},\qquad\kappa=W_{c}[F_{3};H]+b_{c}.

Here rowmax​(F)c,i,j=maxj′⁡Fc,i,j′\mathrm{rowmax}(F)_{c,i,j}=\max_{j^{\prime}}F_{c,i,j^{\prime}} and colmax​(F)c,i,j=maxi′⁡Fc,i′,j\mathrm{colmax}(F)_{c,i,j}=\max_{i^{\prime}}F_{c,i^{\prime},j} broadcast each row’s and column’s maximum, max\max and mean\mathrm{mean} in gg pool over the 64×6464\times 64 positions per channel (so gg has 16+16+32+32=9616+16+32+32=96 entries), ℓ\ell are the eight action logits, and κ\kappa is the 64×6464\times 64 click map. Convolution kernels are cross-correlations of shape (out, in, kk, kk) with zero padding that keeps the 64×6464\times 64 resolution. The input x0x_{0} has 19 channels: 16 one-hot colour planes, row/63/63, column/63/63 and a constant 1. The previous-action input a−a^{-} is a one-hot over the eight actions (RESET, ACTION1–ACTION7, zero at episode start), and the memory mm is zero at episode start. Decoding is deterministic: the argmax of ℓ\ell over available actions (unavailable logits are −∞-\infty, and ties go to the lowest index), and, if ACTION6 wins, the argmax cell of the click map κ\kappa (ties go to the first cell in row-major order). A step whose available-action logits are non-finite is recorded as an invalid action rather than decoded.

Variants (operator ablation).

All variants share the tensor schema. full: axial broadcasts and T=128T=128 tied iterations. noaxial: F3=ReLU(W3[:,:32]F2+b3)F_{3}=\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{3}[:,{:}32]\,F_{2}+b_{3}), so the entries W3[:,32:]W_{3}[:,32{:}] are ignored. t8: as full with T=8T=8. Counting the multiply-accumulates of convolutions and dense layers, a step costs 1.32, 1.31 and 0.19 GMAC for full, noaxial and t8. The FreeArch counting rule, which also counts elementwise operations and reductions, gives 1.33 for full.

Numerics and initialisation.

Writers receive an exact NumPy reference of one actor step. Evaluation uses an equivalent batched FP32 PyTorch implementation (Appendix A.9). Tensors returned by a writer are cast to float32, and the number of entries changed by the cast is recorded. Learned baselines start from θ0\theta_{0}: weights drawn uniformly from [−1/f, 1/f][-1/\sqrt{f},\,1/\sqrt{f}], where ff is the fan-in of the tensor, zero biases, and WhW_{h} scaled by 0.10.1 so that the 128-step recurrence starts stable.

Free-architecture language.

A FreeArch network is a list of nodes evaluated in order, each applying one operation to the inputs or to earlier nodes, and a dictionary of named float32 arrays. The inputs are those of the fixed actor and the available-action mask. The operations are convolutions with kernels of size 1, 3, 5 or 7, elementwise ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and absolute value, the elementwise sum, difference, product, maximum and minimum of two tensors, channel concatenation and slicing, row- and column-wise maximum and sum, global maximum and mean, dense layers, the vector versions of the activations, sum, product, concatenation and slicing, and a loop that runs its body a fixed number of times (at most 256) with tied weights. Loops cannot be nested, and the network contains no data-dependent control flow and no argmax. A network may use at most 150k parameters, 1.5 GMAC per step, 1,000 nodes, 10,000 node evaluations per step (a loop body counted per iteration), 512 channels per tensor, 4,096 channels in total and 256 memory units. A convolution or dense layer costs one MAC per weight application, an elementwise binary operation one per output element and a reduction one per input element. Outputs are decoded as for the fixed actor.

Bounded program player.

A NumPy function of the observation, the available-action mask, a memory vector and the previous action returns action scores, click scores and the next memory, decoded as for FreeArch. As in FreeArch, loops have fixed counts of at most 256 iterations and are not nested, and there is no data-dependent Python control flow, scalar extraction or indexing. FreeArch’s caps apply to operations per call, element operations per call, array size (512×64×64512\times 64\times 64 entries), memory and constants. Unlike FreeArch, the operation set also includes division, floor division, modulo, powers, exp, comparisons, bitwise operators, np.where, roll and flip, reshape and transpose, and reductions and contractions (with one constant operand) along any axis, and FreeArch’s limits of 1,000 nodes and 4,096 summed channels are not enforced. A validator and a counting runtime enforce the rules, and violations are invalid artifacts. The comparison with FreeArch is confounded in both directions: the bounded player has broader operations, no node and channel limits and a familiar language, while the FreeArch prompt shows the complete fixed actor and the bounded player’s prompt only a trivial player.

A.2 Episodes, actions and scoring

Observations are 64×6464\times 64 grids of colour ids 0–15. A policy sees only the current frame and the available-action mask. The game object and planner stay inside the evaluator. Level starts are reached by continuous play from the first level, not by a debug initialiser. Every prompt contains the following rules verbatim:

## Episodes and scoring

An episode starts at the beginning of one level (or at a state reached by a few actions into
it) and ends when that level is completed (success), on GAME_OVER, or after
3 x (shortest solution length) + 10 actions. Invalid actions count as wasted steps. RESET
restarts the current level and counts as an action. Success rate over many held-out episodes
is the score.

The action cap of an episode is 3​L+103L+10, where LL is the length of the planner’s certified direct plan from that episode’s start state (Appendix A.7). Every decision, including RESET, invalid actions, timeouts and errors, uses one step of the cap. Losing a life ends an attempt but not the episode, and such events are counted. On the public tier the engine is configured so that RESET restarts only the current level, as on the private tier and as the rules state.

A.3 Prompts

Prompts are identical across writers and differ between families only in the game section. In order, a prompt contains a title, the game section (redacted simulator source and the engine base class, Appendix A.8), the episode rules above, the start observations of the support set as hexadecimal grids (all support levels of template 0 and the first support level of the other support templates) and the task.

  • •

    Weights task. The prompt gives the actor specification (prose, the NumPy reference and the tensor shapes) and asks for build(), which returns every tensor with exactly its shape. It states that the actor must play the game by itself on levels, layouts and visual variants it has never seen, and that behaviour that only replays the support levels will fail. The weights must be constructed by design: no training, optimising, fitting, searching over weights or simulating the game inside build(). It receives no data, may use only numpy, math and pure-Python standard modules, and must finish within 60 s. The reply must explain the implemented mechanism (which channels and units compute what) and contain exactly one Python code block.

  • •

    Python task. It asks for act(obs, available, memory), where memory is a dictionary that persists within one episode, returning within 10 s per step. P-react additionally forbids reimplementing the transition function, simulating future states and searching over action sequences, allows image analysis of the current frame, and sets 50 ms per step.

  • •

    FreeArch and controls. The FreeArch prompts replace the actor specification by the tensor language, its caps and the fixed actor written in it. The prompts of controls A and B add one paragraph with the graph or operation constraint, which the validator enforces. Operator-ablation prompts add one paragraph that describes the variant.

  • •

    Repair of RL actors. The task asks for edit(params) under the same prohibitions and gives a per-tensor summary of the trained weights (shape, ℓ2\ell_{2} norm, maximum magnitude, nonzero count). The full arrays are passed to edit() at run time. A second interface (three runs per writer and family, like the first) adds the full values of the small output, memory and readout tensors and per-channel statistics of the convolutional and encoder tensors. Per family, Astra and Sol 6.1 reach 0.60–0.89 with the summary and 0.27–0.96 with the values, and Opus 5.5 0.00–0.03 with either.

Feedback rounds (W2, FreeArch W2, P2).

After each submission the artifact is evaluated on S-start (on the public tier, on S-start and S-dev). The feedback message contains a table with template, level, start type, result and action count for every episode, and up to three failure reports. Each report gives the reason (artifact error, invalid action, an action without effect, a return to an earlier frame, or the cap), the first 40 actions, the frame at the first problem, and, for weights, the logits, the value and location of the maximum of every F3F_{3} and HH channel, and the memory norm at that frame. A session stops early once all support episodes are solved. The final artifact is the candidate with the most support successes, ties going to the latest round.

A.4 Writer settings

The writers are GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI) and Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5 (Anthropic), queried in November 2026 through hosted APIs, with no tools, in stateless sessions: every turn resends the full visible transcript, and no hidden reasoning is carried between turns.

  • •

    Effort and output cap. Reasoning effort high (medium in the effort ablation) and an output cap of 128,000 tokens for every writer. A request is cancelled after 90 minutes and not resubmitted.

  • •

    Claude writers (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 5): streaming, adaptive thinking, and an advisory task budget of 96,000 tokens (beta task-budgets-2026-03-13). The model sees a countdown of its remaining budget, which is not enforced. The enforced limit is the 128k output cap, of which the model is not informed.

  • •

    OpenAI writers (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol): background requests, polled every 15 s.

  • •

    Code extraction. The last fenced Python block of the reply is executed, and a reply without one is an invalid artifact.

Prompts were piloted on a toy game with all nine writers and on one family outside the study with GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5. A preliminary study then ran all nine writers under W1 and P1, and the seven current ones also under W2 and P2, on the three study families named in Section 3.1 and another family outside the study, with the solver code in the source and an earlier level split. Its results informed the protocol and prompts of the main study. No output from these runs entered any evaluated prompt.

A.5 Sandbox rules

Writer code is audited statically and then executed in isolation. The threat model is a non-adversarial writer that might accidentally read data, fit parameters or embed tables.

  • •

    Import allowlist (checked in the AST and by an import hook at run time): numpy, math, itertools, functools, collections, heapq, random, dataclasses, typing, enum, copy, operator, statistics, bisect, time, array, re, string, fractions, numbers, abc, warnings, struct and decimal. Relative imports are rejected.

  • •

    Rejected: open, exec, eval, compile, __import__, input, breakpoint, globals, locals, vars, memoryview, exit, quit, help, getattr, setattr, delattr, ctypes, system and popen, every name or attribute that starts with a double underscore, NumPy file input and output (load, save, fromfile, tofile, memmap and related) and a missing entry function.

  • •

    Flagged (recorded, not rejected): linear-algebra solvers and decompositions (lstsq, solve, pinv, inv, svd, eig and related), while loops, more than 1,000 numeric literals, and initialisers that use more than 30 s of CPU time. Flags are assigned by these static checks of the initialiser code, never by hand. A flag never changes a score, and no artifact was excluded for one. Of the 3,719 delivered network artifacts (final artifacts of fixed-actor, FreeArch and repair sessions), 210 carry a flag: 193 for a while loop, 14 for numeric literals and 5 for a linear-algebra routine. Excluding them changes no cell by more than 0.023.

  • •

    Isolation. A separate python -I process in an empty working directory, a new session, a scrubbed environment (single-threaded numerical libraries), restricted builtins, and no data passed in: build() receives nothing and edit() only float32 copies of the trained tensors.

  • •

    Time limits. build() and edit(): 60 s in the prompt, enforced as a 120 s wall-clock and CPU limit. Python players run in one fresh process per episode, so no memory survives between episodes, with 10 s per step and 600 s of CPU per episode. P-react: 50 ms per step in the prompt and a 100 ms hard limit. P-react’s other restrictions are stated in the prompt and audited by source-pattern flags, not enforced by rejection: 56 of the 138 delivered P-react players contain a flagged queue, heap or step function (the prompt allows distances and connected regions in the current frame), and the main writers’ flagged players score no higher than the others (0.38 against 0.44, mean over players). A timeout, crash or exception inside act counts as an invalid action.

  • •

    Output validation. The returned dictionary must contain exactly the tensor names of Table 5 (or of the writer’s FreeArch graph), with exact shapes and finite values after the float32 cast. Otherwise the artifact is invalid.

A.6 Learned baselines

All fixed-architecture learned baselines train the actor of Table 5 from θ0\theta_{0} and are deployed with the same greedy decoding as written actors. Training episodes are S-start and S-dev (support levels and templates only). BC-oracle instead uses every level and all ten templates, each with its level start and three certified perturbed starts. Table 6 lists the hyperparameters. Seeds per family are 3 for BC-support, BC-aug and PPO-shaped, 1 for dihedral-only BC and BC-oracle, one student per Astra and Sol 6.1 run-0 player for both distillation variants, and for PPO 3 on the six ablation families and 1 elsewhere (32 runs).

DAgger (BC and distillation).

DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) runs seven collection rounds. Round 0 follows the teacher, and round i≥1i\geq 1 follows it with probability 0.5i0.5^{i} and the student otherwise. Every visited state is labelled by the teacher, and each round is followed by four epochs of training. The loss is the cross-entropy of the teacher’s action over available actions plus, for ACTION6 labels, the cross-entropy of the clicked cell over the click map. States the planner teacher cannot label within its 5 s budget are dropped from the loss, still feed the memory, and are counted. The distillation teacher is the writer’s final P2 player, run in the sandbox.

Recurrent and progressive training.

Learners use truncated backpropagation through time over windows of 16 steps through the episodic memory. Windows are cut from contiguous episode segments with a random offset per episode and epoch, and are unrolled from the student’s memory at the window start. That memory is recomputed at every epoch by running the current student over the same episode prefix, with the episode’s augmentation applied to every frame, so a window never starts from a memory computed on different frames or by an earlier student. A minibatch holds 4 windows for DAgger (64 frames) and 64 for PPO (1,024 frames). DAgger learners use a simplified progressive loss (Bansal et al., 2022): with probability 0.5 per minibatch, the tied block runs n∼𝒰​{0,…,T−1}n\sim\mathcal{U}\{0,\dots,T-1\} iterations without gradient and k∼𝒰​{1,…,T−n}k\sim\mathcal{U}\{1,\dots,T-n\} with gradient, and the loss is computed on the output after n+kn+k iterations. Otherwise all T=128T=128 iterations run with gradient. Deployment always uses T=128T=128. PPO does not use the progressive loss, because it would change the sampled policy and bias the importance ratio.

Source-licensed augmentation (BC-aug, distill-aug).

Two transformation families are applied to training minibatches only, one per sample or window: (i) a random permutation of the 16 colour ids and (ii) one of the eight elements of the dihedral group D4D_{4} acting on the frame, with ACTION1–ACTION4 remapped as screen directions, click coordinates mapped like pixels, and the available-action mask and previous-action input permuted accordingly. A transformation is licensed only when the game source shows it to preserve semantics. Palette permutation is licensed for all private families. The dihedral group is licensed only where the family’s own templates apply board symmetries that generate D4D_{4} and ACTION1–ACTION4 are absent or are screen directions: lys, esm, aiv, obn, qwv, ubr, trx, qpv, yiy, crg, bvn, yuz and mds.

PPO.

PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) with generalised advantage estimation (Schulman et al., 2015) and a separate critic used only in training: two 4×44\times 4 convolutions with stride 4 over the one-hot frame (32 and 64 channels), concatenated with the actor’s memory and previous action, and a 256-unit hidden layer. Episodes are drawn uniformly from S-start and S-dev. Actions and click cells are sampled during rollouts, and evaluation is greedy. The sparse reward is +1+1 on level completion. The shaped reward adds γ​Φ​(s′)−Φ⁡(s)\gamma\Phi(s^{\prime})-\Phi(s) (Ng et al., 1999) with Φ⁡(s)=−d⁡(s)\Phi(s)=-d(s), the tightest certified planner distance to go within 200 ms, and Φ=0\Phi=0 at every episode end. In all 18 PPO-shaped runs and all shaped-reward runs from written initialisations, every potential was certified. Learning rate and entropy coefficient were selected from {10−4,3⋅10−4}×{0.003,0.01}\{10^{-4},3\cdot 10^{-4}\}\times\{0.003,0.01\} in 1M-step runs on lys, ruz and crg, separately for each reward.

RL from written initialisations.

On the six ablation families with three seeds, PPO starts from the final W2 actor (run 0) of GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6.1 Terra, from θ0\theta_{0}, or from random weights matched to the written actor’s per-tensor nonzero count and ℓ2\ell_{2} norm, for 300k steps with the settings above and each reward. The variants are (a) standard PPO, (b) structure-preserving PPO, which updates only entries that are nonzero at initialisation, adds 0.05KL(π∥πinit)0.05\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{init}}) and trains only the critic for the first 50k steps, (c) SGD on the actor with learning rate 10−510^{-5}, and (d) standard PPO after output-head calibration, which divides WoW_{o} and bob_{o} so that the maximum absolute logit on support starts is 5. Variant (d) runs for the 12 of 18 written actors whose divisor exceeds 1. Every initialisation is evaluated under greedy and sampled decoding. Greedy checkpoints follow at the first update boundary after 10k, 40k, 80k, 160k and 300k steps (16k, 41k, 82k, 164k and 303k). Of the 540 runs, 114 diverged to non-finite weights: 29 of 108 standard-PPO, 8 of 108 structure-preserving, 10 of 72 calibrated and 67 of 108 matched-random runs, and none of the 108 SGD or 36 θ0\theta_{0} runs. Two properties of the written initialisations may add to the collapse. Under the TF32 numerics of training, the written actors solve 56% of support starts greedily (70% in exact FP32) but only 36% when actions are sampled, the mode PPO trains in, and 21% of all runs diverge.

A.7 Evaluation-set construction

All sets are built mechanically from the games’ own levels and renderer templates, without level generators, and are fixed before the main study’s first writer call. Table 7 lists the private families and Table 8 the sets.

  • •

    Templates and palettes (private tier). Seed ss renders with template smod10s\bmod 10. Seeds 0–4 are support and seeds 5–9 held-out templates. Seeds 10–19 permute the palette and are used only where the palette changes the frame. trx has eight templates, so only its seeds 5–7 count as held-out templates. The ten templates are a curated set, not a product of options: in 16 of the 20 families at least one held-out template takes a value on some appearance axis that no support template uses, and in 14 it uses a colour id that no support template uses. The colour ids carrying a given role differ across templates in all 20 families and across palette seeds in 19. Re-rendering one state under another template changes 3–99% of its cells (median over families of the smallest and largest change).

  • •

    Perturbed starts. From the level start, k∼𝒰​{1,…,6}k\sim\mathcal{U}\{1,\dots,6\} moves are drawn uniformly from the moves that change the observation (clicks are probed on up to 48 non-background cells). A candidate is rejected if the prefix completes the level, leaves it or ends an attempt, or if its frame duplicates an existing start. It is kept only if the planner’s direct plan from that state (no RESET, 5 s budget) replays to completion in the native environment. Each requested start gets at most 40 tries. Sets are drawn in the order S-dev, Q-off, Q-lvl, Q-tpl with a shared exclusion set, so no two sets share a start state.

  • •

    Certification and cap. Every start, including the level starts, must certify. Its certified plan length LL sets the action cap 3​L+103L+10. Planner outputs are used only to certify starts and to supervise or shape learned baselines. No plan is shown to a writer.

Public tier.

The 25 official games are provisioned at pinned versions. The longest redacted section has about 126k tokens, mostly literal pixel arrays. Attempt ends are detected from the games’ own signals, including lost lives. Every level start certifies. Of the 3,353 perturbed-state certification checks recorded in the public manifests, 2,675 succeed (79.8%); duplicates and invalid perturbations are rejected before certification. Only certified starts are evaluated. Q-lvl reaches 21 starts per held-out level except for g50t level 3 (16 starts) and wa30 level 9 (11 starts), where the construction budget was exhausted. Augmentation licences come from a per-game source survey and are conservative: palette permutation for 15 and the dihedral group for 4 of the 25 games.

A.8 Redaction procedure

The prompt contains a redacted copy of each family’s simulator source, while the harness keeps using the full source to enter levels and certify starts. The redacted source keeps state, transitions, the goal test, rendering, the level schema, support-level data and the engine base class. Each source file is redacted in five steps:

  1. 1.

    Classes of other families that share the file are replaced by a one-line note.

  2. 2.

    Held-out entries of per-level data and renderer-template tables become WITHHELD placeholders, which the prompt defines as evaluation-only entries. Branches conditioned on a held-out level raise an error. Every function that matches solver, planner, oracle, search or solution patterns is removed with every helper that only it uses, as are statements that store solver output and comments that name solvers, optimal solutions or held-out levels. Mechanics gated by a level index remain visible, because they are rules.

  3. 3.

    Solver-derived quantities in the mechanics are replaced. Oracle move budgets become explicit per-level tables, with support values copied and held-out entries withheld. Support-level slack fields are dropped, because budget minus slack would reveal the optimum. Loss rules or animations that need a search call engine hooks, whose implementation is withheld and whose docstring states exactly what they compute.

  4. 4.

    Comments and prose strings inside per-level data are removed, and the level data itself is unchanged.

  5. 5.

    Every top-level definition that the simulator class cannot reach is dropped (baselines, diagnostics, probes, constants used only by held-out levels, unused imports).

The M+S ablation applies the same redaction of levels and templates but keeps the solver code. The game section opens with a fixed header that names the withheld levels and templates, states that solver and planning code is not included, describes any engine hooks, and explains the start states and template seeds.

Checks and audits.

Every redacted family must compile with no undefined names, reproduce the original simulator frame for frame on every support level and template under certified, perturbed and random action sequences, and raise an error for every held-out level and template. An automated scan lists suspicious content (solver-like names, queue-based search over transition functions, optimal move counts, conditionals on the level index, level numbers in comments, per-level parameter tables, embedded solution witnesses). Two separate agent instances then reviewed ten families each. These audits found leaks or broken code in 18 of the 20 automatically redacted families, such as solvers retained because analysis code called them, oracle-depth tables for held-out levels, held-out builder functions shipped in full and, in one family, removed core mechanics. All were corrected before the main study’s first writer call. Public-tier sections come from reviewed per-game configurations plus a traced excerpt of the engine API and pass the same equivalence check. A full read by separate agent instances found and fixed 10 further leaks. On the public tier, generic rules used only by held-out levels and range gates that include a support level are kept, so some held-out move budgets can be inferred.

A.9 Evaluation and integrity

  • •

    Exact FP32. Final evaluation scores use exact FP32; Figure 4 retains training-time TF32 checkpoint scores. With PyTorch’s default TF32 convolutions, 11 of 60 tested written actors change decisions, on 355 of 3,666 steps (9.7%), because written weights often rely on large gains and exact cancellations. The exact batched GPU evaluator agrees with the NumPy reference on 99.7% of 3,513 decisions from 60 written actors (maximum relative logit error 8×10−68\times 10^{-6}, and the remaining differences are ties). Feedback during writing used a backend that matches the reference within 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}. The mechanism ablations also ran on it, because the batched CPU executor is not faithful (for one 128-step flood fill its logits deviate by up to 10.6). Training of learned baselines and RL used TF32, and Section 4.7 reports an exact-FP32 check.

  • •

    Re-runs. A request was retried automatically only if it provably never started. Whole sessions were re-run from scratch only after interruptions, never based on their outcome: 310 of 5,900 sessions (329 discarded attempts), including 25 whose first request failed at the API before any output. Excluding these sessions changes no private-tier W2, P2 or FreeArch W2 cell by more than 0.006.

  • •

    Missing artifacts. Refusals, truncated replies, invalid artifacts and undelivered sessions score 0. In feedback sessions, a failed round keeps the best earlier artifact.

  • •

    Truncated runs. Two PPO baseline runs were truncated, at 1.80M and 1.06M of 2×1062\times 10^{6} steps (Table 6).

  • •

    Accounting. The main study used 11,637 writer requests in final sessions (588M input, 209M output tokens). A usage-policy classifier stopped only Claude Opus 5.5, and only when it wrote weights (17 of its 120 private-tier fixed-actor sessions, 9 other sessions and 3 of 42 RL-repair requests). Table 9 assigns every writer request of the main study to a session. Of the 204 final sessions without an artifact, 168 returned an invalid artifact, 27 were refused, 8 ended with an API error and 1 was truncated. Not counted are the 697 requests of the prompt pilots and the preliminary study, and 112 requests of 28 sessions outside the design, which were discarded unevaluated. The robustness follow-up in Appendix B is reported separately and is not included in these request totals.

Appendix B Additional results

External language-task networks.

For the comparison with Singh et al. (2026), we inspected their repository snapshot retrieved on 10 November 2026. The sample comprises sentiment-sst2, nli-snli, paraphrase-mrpc and trec-coarse, each with haiku55, opus55 and sonnet55 runs s1 and s2 (24 models). We called each model’s build_model(), disabled the separate dev_report diagnostic, and ran no task evaluation. Three constructors failed because the datasets dependency was unavailable: nli-snli-opus55-s2, nli-snli-sonnet55-s1 and trec-coarse-sonnet55-s2. The 21 constructed models contain 252,513,103 parameters. Shares are pooled over parameters, with exact zero, ±1\pm 1, other nonzero integers of magnitude at most 16, and powers of two of magnitude 2−82^{-8}–2162^{16} classified as in our own weight analysis. The pooled zero share is about 99.2%, and about 95.4% of the nonzero parameters fall in the latter three categories.

Robust written weights.

This condition is the W2 session of the main study (fixed actor, mechanics-only source, three feedback rounds) with one added rule: the actor must keep playing well when every tensor receives independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation 10−310^{-3} times its RMS, added to every entry including the zeros. The prompt adds that weights relying on exact cancellations, exact zeros or very large gains usually fail under such noise. Feedback reports the support success of the exact actor and of the actor under one noise draw, with a new draw in every round, and the final round is the one with the most exact plus noisy support successes. Astra, Sol 6.1 and Opus 5.5 wrote three runs on each of the six ablation families. The API repeatedly returned no response for Sol 6.1 on crg and ruz, so Sol 6.1 has one run on crg and none on ruz. Opus 5.5 sessions stopped by the usage-policy classifier (4 of 18) score 0. Table 13 compares the noise curves with the standard W2 runs of the same writers, families and run indices, and Table 14 gives standard PPO from run 0 of both prompts (exact FP32, 300k steps, sparse and planner-shaped reward, three seeds).

PPO’s first update moves the robust weights by 1.0⋅10−31.0\cdot 10^{-3} of their norm (median over the 15 run-0 actors with both prompts), against 2.9⋅10−52.9\cdot 10^{-5} for the standard ones (median over the 12 whose first update stays finite, while the other three diverge to non-finite weights), with similar largest per-tensor changes (1.2⋅10−21.2\cdot 10^{-2} and 1.1⋅10−21.1\cdot 10^{-2}). On the same actors, held-out success is 0.48 at initialisation (standard 0.57), 0.45 under noise of 10−410^{-4} (0.05), 0.10 after PPO’s first update (0.04, with the three diverged runs scored 0) and 0.14 after a random update with the same per-tensor size and support (0.05, over the 12 finite updates). Robust actors are much weaker when actions are sampled, the mode PPO trains in (Astra 0.62 greedy and 0.15 sampled, against 0.61 and 0.40 for its standard actors), but rescaling the output head to a largest logit of 5 does not help: on the nine robust actors that work, held-out success falls from 0.92 to 0.07 after the first update. Robust runs diverge to non-finite weights less often (6 of 96 against 23 of 102), and none beats both its initialisation and RL(θ0\theta_{0}).

Ablations.

In Table 21, solver code in the source gives Astra 0.53, Sol 0.41 and Opus 0.21, each within the range of single runs without it (Astra 0.22–0.56, Sol 0.31–0.43, Opus 0.06–0.30). Without axial broadcasts, Astra still solves 0.50 and Sol 0.33. With 8 instead of 128 tied iterations, Astra drops to 0.16 and Sol to 0.28, while Opus 5.5 does not drop (0.23, with 3 of 6 sessions delivered). With effort medium, Astra and Sol lose 4–10 points and Terra drops from 0.27 to 0.09. Opus 5.5 scores 0.18 against 0.15, and the three other current writers stay below 0.08 at either effort.

Learned FreeArch networks.

In Table 17, Astra’s FreeArch graphs with re-initialised weights solve 1% of support starts and 1% of held-out-level episodes under either learner, against 100% and 89% with the written weights (higher in 19 of 20 families, tied in the family where the written network also fails). The same learners fit the support set in the fixed actor (90–96%). With random weights, 9 of the 20 graphs have at least 99% of weight entries without gradient on support frames, because an early clamp is inactive everywhere, and one is numerically unstable from the start. Four BC and five distillation runs diverged and score 0, and seven reached the time limit.

Cost and latency.

We timed 120 FreeArch actors drawn at random from the 451 above, 60 fixed-actor written actors and 60 Python players, in exact FP32 on one otherwise idle GPU (Table 25, Appendix B). The FreeArch networks have fewer parameters and MACs than the fixed actor, but they evaluate a median of 2,362 small nodes per step, against 412. At batch 1 in matched eager mode they are 5×\times slower (24 against 4.8 ms); batched, they cost 525 μ\mus per action against 273 μ\mus. Sandboxed Python players take a median of 0.8 ms per call on one CPU thread, where both network types need about 36 ms. Written networks are thus not cheaper per step than programs, only static and bounded.

Reactive programs (P-react).

P-react is a one-shot program control without simulation or search (one run per family; Appendix A.5). Pooled over the main writers, it solves 40%: above one-shot written weights (27%), close to written weights with feedback (42%), and far below unrestricted programs (99%). Because P-react forbids search while the fixed actor iterates its tied block 128 times, it is not matched to the actor’s computation and does not separate understanding the rules from expressing them.

Structure of the Python players.

Of the final unrestricted programs (P2), only 7–39% (by writer) contain explicit queue-based search and up to 29% re-implement transition steps. Most parse the state and compute the answer directly.

Mechanism.

In five strong written actors (Astra and Sol 6.1; two easy, two medium and one hard family), we ablated the components the writers name, after writing down the predicted effect. 14 of 17 predictions were confirmed; each of the 3 misses failed on one metric. Zeroing the tied-block channels the writer calls a flood fill, in a maze family, drops held-out success from 0.97 to 0. In the hard family, zeroing the channels described as value propagation drops it from 1.0 to 0.04. Zeroing one direction latch in memory leaves unperturbed starts at 1.0 but halves success on perturbed starts. The networks are very sparse: 1.4–13.8% of weights are nonzero, the tied block uses 2–16 channels and memory at most 7 of 64 units. FreeArch networks are closed-loop as well (family means per writer): frozen at the first frame, they solve 5–8% of held-out-level episodes, and the chosen action changes on 72–76% of counterfactual frames.

From RL to written weights.

Asked to repair the 2M-step PPO-shaped actors of two families (held-out success 0.00 and 0.03) through edit(params), shown a per-tensor summary or also the small tensors’ values (Appendix A.3), Astra and Sol 6.1 rebuild them (21 of 23 actors change more than 99.9% of entries) and reach 0.27–0.96, like their fresh W2 actors (0.32–0.92); Opus 5.5 makes small edits and never exceeds the RL actor. Continued PPO stays at 0.00–0.01.

Preliminary-study families.

Table 20 repeats the main comparisons without the three study families of the preliminary study. On the remaining 17 families, the H3 trend test gives Spearman ρ=0.59\rho=0.59 (one-sided permutation p=0.007p=0.007), against ρ=0.67\rho=0.67 (p<0.001p<0.001) on all 20. The three families are 3 of the 6 ablation families and 3 of the 5 mechanism actors (Section 4.5). On the other three ablation families (ruz, crg, mds), one-shot written weights solve at most 0.13 in every ablation arm, so the ablation contrasts come almost entirely from the preliminary-study families.

Protocol-specified secondary analyses.

Table 18 reports delivery, the analyses conditional on delivery and without undelivered sessions, Q-pal and the number of runs that reach 0.5. With feedback, only Opus 5.5 has undelivered sessions (8 in W2, 1 in FreeArch W2). Without them, its W2 rises from 0.36 to 0.39–0.41. In the one-shot arms, where delivery is lower, excluding undelivered sessions raises Opus 5.5’s W1 from 0.15 to 0.18 and Sol 6.1’s FreeArch W1 from 0.52 to 0.67, and changes every other main-writer cell by at most 0.03. Q-pal is within 5 points of Q-lvl in every cell, but it contains only level starts and 19 families, so the difference is not a matched palette effect. The last analysis compares feedback with choosing the best of kk one-shot runs by support-start success (ties going to the first run) at the same token cost, where kk is the rounded ratio of the mean tokens of a W2 session to those of a W1 session. At matched output tokens the ratio is 2.1–3.5, so k=2k=2 for Astra and Sol 6.1 and k=3k=3 for Opus 5.5 and Terra, with best-of-2 averaged over the three pairs of runs. Best-of-kk then reaches 0.48, 0.35, 0.24 and 0.27, against 0.56, 0.43, 0.36 and 0.33 for W2. At matched total tokens (input and output) the ratio is 3.4–5.1, so kk would exceed the three one-shot runs per family except for Astra. Best-of-3, which uses 59–88% of W2’s total tokens, gives 0.51, 0.37, 0.24 and 0.27.
